youtube.title: The slow raindrop | Reality Rulebook Season 2 · Episode 6
youtube.caption:
How fast is rain? It starts far above, in clouds. A stone keeps speeding up, but a raindrop doesn't: the air pushes back harder the faster it falls, until the push matches its weight, and then the speed stays the same. Bigger drops fall faster, and the biggest flatten and break apart. In our simple model, a one-millimeter drop tops out near 5 meters a second and a four-millimeter drop near 9.

That's season two. Season 2 · Episode 6.

Sources
1. Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (text read by the builder, not yet by a person): https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09570
2. OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 6.4 'Drag Force and Terminal Speed' (read, 9 Nov 2026): https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/6-4-drag-force-and-terminal-speed
3. Our own simple model of the falling drop (compile.py and scene.mjs; made-up round numbers, drag coefficient 0.5; the 'real drops near 9 m/s' check is from memory and not opened): https://github.com/arzateruben22/Claude/tree/claude/physics-s2/films/channels/physics/ep12

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Animation: code-rendered, no stock footage. The speeds come from our own simple model (round drops, made-up round numbers); the flattening and the break-up, and the rain at the end, are illustrations, not simulations. The fall is slowed 4x. The sources were read by the builder, not yet opened by a person.

Reality Rulebook: Everyday things, slowed down until the physics shows.
